repos.title: Fast and Accurate Hand Estimation in Pixels, Interaction and World Space
repos.paper_summary: FAH is a family of hand-pose models built on SAM 3D Body's hand branch. The method predicts corresponding 2D and 3D hand joints and surface points with a heatmap head, then fits MANO or MHR-Hand meshes in a separate stage. Optional heads estimate anatomical parts and contact without object geometry at inference, a causal refiner smooths video tracks, and a camera model places hands in world space. In a controlled comparison within one network, directly predicted 3D points gave better mesh accuracy than predicting MANO parameters. On HOT3D v1, FAH-L reaches 4.31 mm PA-MPJPE and 8.89 mm root error at 65 fps with mesh fitting on an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER, against 6.72 mm PA for WiLoR and 9.46 mm PA for HaMeR (4.6 fps). The smallest model, FAH-S, runs at 101 fps. The paper names camera estimation as the main source of world-space error, and states that contact without object geometry remains ambiguous, with most contact vertices hidden on 96% of HOT3D contact hands.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Rig-based hand estimators propagate articulation errors to 2D landmarks, so FAH predicts points and fits meshes separately.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work regresses mesh parameters or vertices, and some contact methods need object shape and pose.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: FAH distills SAM 3D Body's hand branch into ViT students and predicts dense 2D and 3D points with a heatmap head.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On the egocentric benchmark, the default FAH model's aligned joint error is 4.31 mm, below WiLoR's 6.72 mm.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations and Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Camera estimation dominates world-space error, and contact remains ambiguous without object geometry.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists training sources, teacher and student settings, label conventions, and image credits.

repos.title: Measuring AI Agents as Teammates with Collaborative Intelligence
repos.paper_summary: The Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark measures how well an AI agent works as a teammate, using 240 tasks across 8 teamwork dimensions. Each task comes from a real record or an existing benchmark with a programmatically checkable outcome. Models are scored only on tasks they solve alone, then run in a baseline team with no problems and in a test team where a scripted teammate creates a dimension-specific problem, such as pushing for an unsafe shortcut or withholding a key fact. Code checks the final state, and LLM judges label the model's messages to decide how the scripted teammate responds. Across 18 models, the best overall score is 82.2 out of 100 (Gemini 4 Argon at high reasoning effort), and the default-setting best is 76.6. Frontier models pass at least 93% of unsafe-pressure and misconduct tests but reach the best deal in only 14% of conflicts and pass 45% of emotional-intelligence tests. Models with nearly the same capability differ by up to 11 points as teammates. Judges agree with people on 82.5% of 40 messages (Cohen's κ = 0.81). The public set has 160 tasks and a private held-out set of 80.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Current benchmarks measure models alone, so teamwork needs its own measure, which the paper proposes.

digest_headlines.heading: Benchmark Construction
digest_headlines.headline: Each task runs alone, in a calm team and in the test, and scores count only tasks solved alone.

digest_headlines.heading: How Well Do Models Work as Teammates?
digest_headlines.headline: Open-weight models trail frontier models by 31.2 points on average, and high reasoning effort adds only small gains.

digest_headlines.heading: Failure Modes of Teamwork
digest_headlines.headline: Failures take three forms: missing the problem, giving in after naming it, or naming it without fixing it.

digest_headlines.heading: How Do AI Agents Compare with People as Teammates?
digest_headlines.headline: Models exceed reported human success rates on three of six comparison tasks, and reach the best negotiated deal more often than people.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior multi-agent work evaluates teams as a whole, whereas this paper scores collaboration as one model's ability.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Most failures come after the model has already seen the problem, so the gap lies in acting on it.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix covers limitations, a scripted-teammate example, score validity checks, judge agreement, failure-mode rules and case transcripts.

repos.title: TaoMate-HD: Progressive-Resolution Autoregressive Audio-Video Generation
repos.paper_summary: TaoMate-HD is an autoregressive model for streaming joint audio-video generation at 768×1376 resolution. Each chunk runs three denoising stages: two on a 480×864 grid and a final one on the 768×1376 grid. Each stage's clean prediction is encoded into a stage-specific key/value history bank for the same stage of the next chunk, so the next chunk can start before the previous one finishes refinement. Continuation training uses overlapping text windows and student-generated rollouts, scored by distribution-matching distillation. The model is a rank-128 LoRA trained on 10,000 distillation pairs over MiniMax-H3. On 100 self-constructed sequences of 1–10 minutes, progressive generation runs 1.60× faster than direct 768p generation (4.68 vs 2.93 FPS, serial). Stage-parallel deployment reaches 8.99 FPS, 1.92× the serial rate. Continuation training lowers character error rate from 30.75% to 19.57%. Limitations: the benchmark uses self-constructed sequences, the parallel configuration has slightly higher CER (21.28%), and serial TaoMate-HD's LipSync (7.061) trails MiniMax-H3 (7.569).

digest_headlines.heading: 1 Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: TaoMate-HD targets high-resolution audiovisual streaming, where dense denoising is costly and text updates can repeat or interrupt speech.

digest_headlines.heading: 2 Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers few-step distillation, progressive resolution, and stage-parallel inference, which uses history at stage output noise levels.

digest_headlines.heading: 3 Method
digest_headlines.headline: Chunks denoise in two low-resolution steps and one high-resolution step, with each stage's clean prediction reused as history.

digest_headlines.heading: 4 Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Serial TaoMate-HD scores highest on Temporal and AudioAes among streaming generators, reaching 0.913 and 4.407.

digest_headlines.heading: 5 Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion summarizes gains from progressive denoising and asymmetric distillation, extending to an hour of streaming.

repos.title: EvoMemState: Evolving Memory State for Personal Agents
repos.paper_summary: EvoMemState is a memory framework for LLM personal agents. It keeps each fact with Relational States (its validity, scope, and links such as `SUPERSEDES` and `CONFLICTS_WITH`) and generates a request-specific Reasoning State describing how retrieved facts apply. A GRPO-trained policy produces Reasoning States, with rewards equal to the frozen agent's score with the state minus its score without it, so training needs reference answers. At inference, the system retrieves K similar facts and expands them through memory relations. On MemSyco-Bench, MemTrapBench, LoCoMo, and LoCoMo-Refined, compared with nine memory systems, it reaches an overall average of 59.9 with Qwen3-8B (best baseline 53.6, SimpleMem) and 61.2 with GPT-4o-mini (best baseline 54.2, MemoryBank). Gains are not uniform: with Qwen3-8B, its CogBias accuracy is 62.3, below LightMem's 69.9. The paper states that it covers text-only histories; multimodal memory is future work. The provided text is truncated before the baseline descriptions.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Fact-centric memory systems miss how facts update and conflict, motivating a state-centric framework with three components.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminary Studies
digest_headlines.headline: Preliminary studies find related memories are often not retrieved together, and full retrieval does not ensure correct use.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Method builds an ontology of facts, trains a policy to generate Reasoning States, and reasons over both states.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiment
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments show gains over nine baselines on memory-use and dialogue benchmarks, with each component contributing in ablations.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers personal user modeling and long-term memory systems that maintain and organize user information.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion states that reliable personal memory needs both coherent state construction and use-driven state evolution.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitation
digest_headlines.headline: The method handles only text histories, leaving multimodal personal information such as documents and images for future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Use of Large Language Models
digest_headlines.headline: Authors disclose that large language models were used for English editing and table formatting, with authors reviewing all output.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists frequently asked questions, method details, prompts, extended related work, and figures for case studies and efficiency.

repos.title: Perseus: A Full-Stack System for Homomorphic Model Inference
repos.paper_summary: Perseus is a free, open-source Python library for encrypted (CKKS) model inference, covering the cryptographic backend, data packing, and bootstrap placement. It adds three optimizations, one per level: in-kernel regeneration of key-switching keys from a ChaCha12 seed (halving key storage), a complex-valued extension of Cachemir packing that carries two real vectors per ciphertext (roughly halving memory), and a bootstrap placer that uses packing period and coefficient magnitude, with an iterated minimum cut, to place about 30% fewer bootstraps than comparable placers. On encrypted Llama-3-8B single-token decoding, the paper reports 7.8 s per token on one RTX PRO 6000 at 512 context, which it states is 3.96× faster than Sylph (31.0 s, a composed timing on closed-source HEaaN). Encrypted perplexity is 7.77 against 7.76 in plaintext. Encrypted GPT-2 reaches perplexity 26.46 against 26.47 in plaintext, and 100% normalized next-token accuracy over 64 prompts. Limitations: Llama-3-8B and some competitor timings are composed from per-block measurements rather than run end to end, and the accuracy checks use 64 held-out examples per task.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Perseus is a free open Python library that adds optimizations at every level of encrypted model inference.

digest_headlines.heading: Perseus
digest_headlines.headline: Perseus adds one optimization per stack level: key regeneration, complex-Cachemir packing, and a magnitude-aware bootstrap placer.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Perseus reaches 3.96 times faster single-token decoding on Llama-3-8B and matches plaintext accuracy on the tested models.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Works
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work either regenerates keys only in custom hardware or uses the imaginary half of slots only during prefill.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: Perseus delivers top latency across several models and modalities and opens a public GPT-2 speedrun.

repos.title: Stop Handcrafting Your Engine! GenDB-V: Towards AI-Generated and Formally Verified Database Systems
repos.paper_summary: GenDB-V has AI agents synthesize SQL engines, either per query template or as general-purpose engines, and verify them in Verus against fixed targets generated from SQLSpec, a formal SQL semantics library based on PostgreSQL documentation. Agents co-design storage layouts and execution code, prototype without proofs, then write three-layer proofs: storage reader contracts, physical loop invariants, and bridge lemmas to SQLSpec. An independent Verus pipeline with the Z3 solver checks the proofs before the verified Rust is compiled into a library. On TPC-H at SF100 and SEC-EDGAR at SF3, verified template implementations reach geometric-mean speedups of 22.0–61.3× over DuckDB and Umbra. A verified general-purpose engine reaches total-workload speedups of 1.27–3.4× on TPC-H. Against Bespoke OLAP, an audit and tests found incorrect answers in its implementations for 16 of 28 templates. Limitations: SQLSpec's semantics still need community review, and its coverage excludes window functions and recursive queries. Joint template synthesis costs USD 2,310 across both benchmarks; general engine synthesis costs USD 1,229.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Database engines need costly rebuilds and testing still misses bugs, so GenDB-V has AI agents synthesize engines verified for correctness.

digest_headlines.heading: GenDB-V Overview
digest_headlines.headline: GenDB-V separates correctness targets from agent search, and an independent verifier admits only code that meets the fixed targets.

digest_headlines.heading: Formal Synthesis Targets
digest_headlines.headline: SQLSpec formalizes SQL semantics so fixed synthesis targets can be built deterministically from each SQL workload, outside agent control.

digest_headlines.heading: Joint Code and Proof Synthesis
digest_headlines.headline: Agents co-optimize storage and execution, prototype without proofs, then prove only the fastest design through three modular proof layers.

digest_headlines.heading: Independent Verification
digest_headlines.headline: An isolated Verus pipeline with read-only specifications checks agent proofs and compiles the verified code into a shared library.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Verified template implementations reach geometric-mean speedups of 22.0–61.3× over DuckDB and Umbra across TPC-H and SEC-EDGAR.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior LLM synthesis checks correctness by testing, while concurrent JetStream includes a formally verified stateful variant.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Formal correctness and substantial speedups over established engines together suggest a path toward AI-generated verified database systems.

repos.title: D&A: Decoupling Description and Assessment Enables VLMs as Zero-Shot Robotic Reward Models
repos.paper_summary: D&A (Describe & Assess) is a prompt-only method that uses a frozen vision-language model as a zero-shot reward model for robot videos. A Describer writes a text description of the whole trajectory without seeing the task instruction, which reduces confirmation bias. An Assessor writes a success criterion for the instruction, then scores each timestep of the description from 0 to 1 and can produce failure feedback. Videos are downsampled to 8 frames and the rewards are interpolated back to full length. On RoboRewardBenchmark, D&A has the lowest mean absolute error in Table III (0.70, lower is better), compared with 0.75 for Robometer, 0.85 for RoboReward-4B, and 1.80 for TOPReward. On RBM-EVAL-OOD, Robometer has higher VOC (0.934 vs. 0.885 for D&A). Real-world online and offline RL results are shown only in Fig. 4, without numbers. Limitations: high latency and cost (USD 0.035 and 23.7 s per trajectory with Gemini 3.1 Pro), closed-API stochasticity, occasional hallucinations, and reward granularity bounded by what can be described in language.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Zero-shot vision-language models often hallucinate progress in failed robot runs, and post-training needs costly robot data.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior reward models either post-train on robot data or read progress zero-shot from a single scalar signal.

digest_headlines.heading: Demonstrating Bias in Zero-Shot VLM Prompting
digest_headlines.headline: Direct zero-shot prompting shows confirmation bias, with GPT-5.3 scoring pixel motion instead of task progress on one video.

digest_headlines.heading: D&A: Decoupling Description and Assessment
digest_headlines.headline: D&A splits reward estimation into an instruction-blind description step and a rubric-based assessment step.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: D&A is competitive with post-trained reward models across three benchmarks and improves real-world policy learning.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations and Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: D&A depends on closed frontier models with high latency and token cost, and it cannot express rewards that are hard to verbalize.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers RL derivations, extra benchmark tables, cost and latency, CaP details, the D&A-Bench dataset, and full prompts.

repos.title: Route Anything: A Study of Model and Policy Routing for General-Purpose AI Systems
repos.paper_summary: Route Anything is a unified framework for studying which candidate to call per input across text, image, video, speech, code, agent, and robot-policy tasks. The authors build an omni-modal trajectory matrix of 374,401 scored runs over 452 candidate configurations on 25 benchmarks. A per-input oracle beats the best fixed candidate per benchmark by 5.4 points. Learned routers beat it by 0.3 points across 16 benchmarks and by 2.1 points on video generation. On robot manipulation, a scene-aware router reaches 71.6% success against 70.5% for the best single policy, with 24% less policy time. Against a reference model, routing raises efficiency 8.82× on average and 25.5× on coding. The theory defines router value as expected outcome net of cost, and proves a finite-sample certified quality floor that holds at level α for i.i.d. test inputs. Limitations: most of the matrix has no recorded costs, so most analysis is at zero price, and the cost results rely on specific testbeds.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Routing is posed as choosing one candidate per input across 25 benchmarks and 452 candidate configurations.

digest_headlines.heading: A Router’s Value
digest_headlines.headline: The information a router observes bounds its attainable value, and its optimal form is routing at a single price.

digest_headlines.heading: Can Router Beat the Best Fixed Candidate?
digest_headlines.headline: The per-input oracle scores 87.98 against 82.60 for the best fixed candidate, and most of the gap lies within task types.

digest_headlines.heading: How Well Do Learned Routers Work?
digest_headlines.headline: One learned router scores 79.98 against 79.68 for the fixed candidate across 16 benchmarks and matches it on ten.

digest_headlines.heading: When Is a Cheaper Route Good Enough?
digest_headlines.headline: Routing to cheaper candidates raises efficiency over the reference by 8.82× on average, at a small quality cost.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: The related work places routing alongside cascades, portfolios, and test-time compute, and extends them to image, video, speech, and robot outputs.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Routing gains come chiefly from cheaper routes that are good enough, and three rules follow for comparing and training routers.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives proofs of the theory and extra experiments on verifiers, routing signals, and router memory, and states limitations.

repos.title: EO-Jev: Decision Model for Earth Observation
repos.paper_summary: EO-Jev is a decision model for Earth observation (EO), created by adapting the 8.4B-parameter d3-flash with low-rank adapters (LoRA) trained on public EO training splits. Instead of generating text, it returns a probability over candidate answers in one forward pass. Training minimizes a KL loss against target distributions, plus a ranked probability score on ordinal questions, with about 20% of each batch replaying general decision data. Evaluated on 30 settings from 23 benchmarks, it improves significantly over d3-flash on 26 settings, gaining 23.8 points on average in-domain and 8.0 points on 12 held-out settings. It matches or exceeds the best EO specialist on 20 of 28 settings and has lower expected calibration error (ECE) on 21 of 28. The cost is a 1.8-point drop on the general Decision Index. Limitations: counting remains weak, trailing RSThinker by 7.8 points on NWPU VHR-10; LHRS-Bench strict accuracy falls 5.2 points; and calibration becomes overconfident on some out-of-domain settings. With one question per call, a single forward pass runs a median 3.2× faster than the best specialist.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Decision models return option probabilities in one pass, but their accuracy and calibration on Earth observation are unclear.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation Setup
digest_headlines.headline: The evaluation compares d3-flash, its backbone and specialists on identical questions across 30 settings from public benchmarks.

digest_headlines.heading: How Far Does a General Decision Model Reach on EO?
digest_headlines.headline: A general decision model transfers well on multiple-choice reasoning but trails on counting, change, damage and absent objects.

digest_headlines.heading: What Does EO Supervision Add?
digest_headlines.headline: EO adaptation lifts in-domain and held-out settings, matching or exceeding specialists on 20 of 28 settings at a 1.8 point general cost.

digest_headlines.heading: Can the Model’s Confidence Be Trusted, and at What Cost?
digest_headlines.headline: EO-Jev's calibration error is lower than specialists' on 21 of 28 settings, and its single pass is faster.

digest_headlines.heading: What Remains Hard?
digest_headlines.headline: Counting on unseen imagery, option-order consistency, cross-view geometry and overconfidence under shift remain unresolved.

digest_headlines.heading: Where Does a Decision Model Stand on EO?
digest_headlines.headline: A calibrated decision model can serve as the default EO interface, with uncertain answers deferred to specialists.

digest_headlines.heading: Additional Evaluation Details
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists benchmarks, specialist references, output processing, EO-Jev training sources and the timing protocol.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Adapting d3-flash yields EO-Jev, which improves 26 settings at a 1.8 point cost in general decision performance.

repos.title: VidDub: Replacement-Aware Distillation for Two-Step Video Dubbing
repos.paper_summary: VidDub is a two-step diffusion model for video dubbing, which replaces the lip movements in a source video to match new speech while keeping identity, head pose, and background. Its main training change, replacement-aware cross-audio supervision, masks out source-mouth reconstruction losses on unpaired replacement-audio clips and supervises the mouth only through an audio–visual synchronization loss (LatentSync-1.6 StableSyncNet). A 48-step full-context teacher, built on Wan-1.3B with VACE conditioning and a 287M audio adapter, is distilled into a two-step student by trajectory regression on 4,096 frozen trajectories, then refined with distribution matching distillation. On the paper's VidDub-Bench (256 generated videos), the two-step model reports replacement Sync-C 8.709 and FVD 17.50 in Table 3, with 11.3 FPS on one H20. On HDTF, it reports replacement Sync-C 10.102 and FVD 27.66 (Table 1), compared with 8.160 and 28.05 for LatentSync 1.6 at 20 NFE. Across three seeds, the masking reduces cross-audio Sync-C by 0.833±0.040 relative to the unmasked variant. Limitations: the benchmark is generated video, and the paper reports that block-causal streaming has higher first-frame latency than the full-context model.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Same-audio reconstruction training conflicts with replacement-speech dubbing, so the paper masks conflicting mouth losses and distills to two steps.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work contrasts same-audio reconstruction training and causal streaming with offline full-window two-step editing.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Source-mouth losses are masked under replacement audio, and a full-context teacher is distilled into a two-step student.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Masking conflicting mouth loss raises cross-audio Sync-C in ablations, and the final model has the lowest external visual-only word error rate.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion summarizes VidDub's two components and claims combined articulation accuracy, identity preservation, and stable minute-long output.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists data splits, causal-variant comparisons, long-video and human-study tables, qualitative figures, and ethical safeguards.
